storyTitle: American Culture Ate the World
text:
>This article includes some essential details that are largely unknown to most readers: the US government not only severely restricted the ability of foreigners to even enter the United States based on ideology and national origin
Is there a country in the world that doesn't do this? I understand that some people want some sort of borderless society, but support for this is basically a fringe belief in every country.
>they also severely restricted the ability of Americans to LEAVE THEIR OWN COUNTRY, again based upon ideology and "race" (see the case of the Black American journalist whose passport was revoked because he dared to report from Cuba!)
It's worth noting that the courts have ruled that such restrictions were unlawful. Given that, it seems like the system was working as expected?
>The greatest triumph of the American system of doctrinal management has been the inculcation of the bedrock belief that "we live in a free society." We do not, and we never have.
The problem with this argument is that it hinges on the definition of "free society", and therefore any discussion over it is inevitably going to end up arguing over what "free society" means. It's trivial to make the same statement about other country that's allegedly a "free society". eg.
"Sweden is a free society."
"Actually no, how can you even claim that? They have hate speech laws which severely limit your ability to make unorthodox views on race/gender. Only the US (which has no hate speech laws) is a free society!"
>Would a "free" country jail its citizens at a rate FIVE TIMES HIGHER than the other countries of the world?
Perhaps, depending on how strongly it feels about crime. For instance, Taiwan has incarceration rate that's roughly twice of China. Does that mean it's not a free country? Or is a 2x factor small enough to let slide?
>Would a "free" country maintain police forces in every major city that are larger and more well-equipped than most national armies worldwide?
That sounds surprising until you realize that:
1. many metrics relating to size follow a pareto distribution, so not surprising at all that "major cities" in the US exceed the median country in some metric. For instance, if we look at GDP, we see that the median "country/territory"[1] has a gdp of 26.461 billion. If we compare that to data from the BEA[2], we see that there's a whopping 113 metropolitan statistical areas that exceed the median "country/territory" GDP.
2. "national armies" tend to be smaller than "police officers" in most countries, which make the criteria even easier to fulfill.

What a trite and naïve rephrasing of Mazlow's Hierarchy of Needs (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maslows_hierarchy_of_needs ).  I will certainly grant that Economists and Business people need to have these ideas battered into their thick crania, however it's irritating to have the speaker present ideas as if they were novel which are not only not novel, but actually thousands of years old.
If you pay people well enough to decouple their concerns about economic survival from their work, it shouldn't be surprising that there isn't a relationship between increased reward leading to increased performance.  That's a pretty fundamental part of the humanist movement which predates the French and American Revolutions (Liberté, égalité, fraternité! or Americans might prefer Life, Liberty and the Pursuit of Happiness).  Even then, Humanism was merely the popularization and egalitarian movement to provide for everyone the model which the wealthy and elite have been following since at least the time of Aristotle!
Put succinctly, this guy isn't describing the Open Source movement, he's describing at least 2500 years of Academia.  You pay people a tenured salary, because they, free of concerns regarding economic security, will produce works for the benefit of all.
And this is telling for two reasons.  First, Academia is not free from woe and misery. author: jfengel
storyTitle: Why are presidential elections so close to 50–50?
text:
Because of the Median Voter Theorem:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median_voter_theorem
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duverger%27s_law
It's not as one-dimensional as the theorem says, but it works out the same way. Parties are collections of diverse interests that agree to work together. The interests are multidimensional but the results are not: you either win or you lose.
If you lose, you change your party (or coalition of parties) to appeal more widely. (Or don't, and continue to lose.) If you win, you want your coalition to be as small as possible over 50%, because the more people you add, the more conflicts you have to resolve.
Real life is never as simple as the axioms that lead to the theorems, but they enough to make it unsurprising that most large-scale elections are close. (The smaller the scale, the more likely some other assumptions will dominate.)

author: tusharchoudhary
storyTitle: A new theory about political polarization
text:
Political science seems to be going through a phase of questioning the rationality of voters.
The two major theories of public choice -- Median Voter theory[1] (political parties take positions that appeal to the median voter) and Investment theory of Party Competition[2] (parties take positions most beneficial to their donors), both assume emotions (irrationality) of voters to be small. In the current political climate -- while it seems that the explanatory power of emotions seems to have gone up, it isn't clear why.
This sounds very similar to the debate in economics around Efficient market hypothesis[3] and the emergence of behavioral economists.
While it is seems easy to attribute things to emotion, we might miss other explanatory variables underneath. A great sound-bite from Thomas Ferguson who first proposed [2]: "The electorate is not too stupid or too tired to control the political system. It is merely too poor."
